The longitudinal development of large-scale functional brain networks for arithmetic ability from childhood to adolescence
Eur J Neurosci. 2022;55:1825–1839.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/ejn.15651
© 2022 Federation of European Neuroscience Societies and John Wiley & Sons Ltd

Arithmetic ability is an important high-level cognitive function that requires interaction among multiple brain regions. Previous studies on arithmetic development have focused on task-induced activation in isolated brain regions or functional connectivity among particular seed regions. However, it remains largely unknown whether and how functional connectivity among large-scale brain modules contributes to arithmetic development. In the present study, we used a longitudinal sample of task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data comprising 63 typically developing children, with two testing points being about 2 years apart. With graph theory, we examined the longitudinal development of large-scale brain modules for a multiplication task in younger (mean age 9.88 at time 1) and older children (mean age 12.34 at time 1), respectively. The results showed that the default-mode (DMN) and frontal-parietal networks (FPN) became increasingly segregated over time. Specifically, intra-connectivity within the DMN and FPN increased significantly with age, and inter-connectivity between the DMN and visual network decreased significantly with age. Such developmental changes were mainly observed in the younger children but not in the older children. Moreover, the change in network segregation of the DMN was positively correlated with longitudinal gain in arithmetic performance in the younger children, and individual difference in network segregation of the FPN was positively correlated with arithmetic performance at Time 2 in the older children.

A total of 63 typically developing children aged 8–15 years were tested twice, with testing sessions being about 2 years apart. All participants were native English speakers, right-handed and were reported to have normal hearing, normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders. Nine children were excluded, of whom six with excessive head movements in the MRI scanner (exceeding 3.0 mm in displacement or 3° in rotation) and three with inside-scanner task accuracy being below 50% either at Time 1 (T1) or at Time 2 (T2), yielding 54 children in the final sample. Two groups were created based on the median-split of participant’s age at Time 1: younger group and older group. The two groups differed significantly in age both at T1 and T2, with no differences in gender distribution, time between sessions and intelligence scores. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Review Board of Hangzhou Normal University.

Data in the present study were taken from a public neuroimaging dataset entitled ‘Brain Correlates of Math Development’. This dataset has been deposited in the OpenNeuro (https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds001486/versions/1.3.0).

The inside-scanner task involved 72 single-digit multiplication problems: 48 with correct solutions and 24 with false solutions. Problems involving zero, one or ties (e.g., 3 × 3) were not included. In each trial, the multiplication problem and proposed solution were presented successively on a white background for 800 ms, separated by an inter-stimulus interval for 200 ms. Then a red fixation square was displayed for 2200, 2600 or 3000 ms. Participants were instructed to respond with their index finger if the proposed solution of the multiplication problem was correct and with their middle finger if the solution was incorrect. To control for motor responses, 24 control trials were designed, where a blue square was presented for 800 ms, followed by a red fixation square lasting 2200, 2600 or 3000 ms. The total scanning lasted about 8 min. Reaction time and accuracy were recorded for each trial.

The outside-scanner task was the multiplication subtest of the Comprehensive Mathematical Abilities Test (CMAT). It was a paper-and-pencil test with no time limits. For each participant, the number of correct answers was used as an estimate of multiplication ability.

Whole-brain imaging was performed on a Siemens 3T TIM Trio MRI scanner using a 32-channel head coil. For each subject, BOLD-sensitive T2*-weighted functional images were acquired using a susceptibility weighted single-shot echo planar imaging sequence (repetition time = 2000 ms, echo time = 20 ms, flip angle = 80°, field of view = 220 × 206.25 mm, matrix size = 128 × 120, slice thickness/gap = 3/0.48 mm and slice number = 32). Prior to functional image acquisition, a high-resolution 3D structural image was acquired for anatomic normalization (repetition time = 2300 ms, echo time = 3.36 ms, matrix size = 256 × 256, field of view = 240 mm, slice thickness = 1 mm and slice number = 160).

In the present study, we preprocessed the raw imaging data using SPM12. First, the first six functional images of each participant were discarded due to instability of initial MR signals. Then, the imaging data were preprocessed with reorientation to the anterior–posterior commissure line, slice time correction and head-motion correction. The individual high-resolution structural image of each participant was co-registered with the mean functional image. Grey matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid were segmented using the SPM12 New Segmentation procedure. A child template was created by the Template-O-Matic toolbox and used in the New Segment procedure. Subsequently, the DARTEL tool was applied to normalize each participant’s high-resolution structural image to the Montreal Neurological Institute space, and the normalization parameters were applied to the functional images. Finally, spatial smoothing was conducted using a 6-mm full-width half-maximum Gaussian kernel. A censoring/scrubbing strategy was used to remove time points with frame-wise displacement (FD) greater than 0.3 mm. Thereafter, three additional processes were applied before calculating brain connectivity measures: (1) high-pass filtering with a cut-off frequency of 1/128 Hz; (2) linear detrending; (3) regression of the first five principal components of white-matter and cerebrospinal fluid signals, six motion parameters and their temporal first-order derivatives.

We first analysed the changes in behavioural performance over time for the children by running a Group (younger, older) × Time (T1, T2) repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA). Follow-up tests included paired and independent-samples t tests as appropriate.

Recently, characterizing functional connectivity between
large-scale brain modules has become an emerging
approach for investigating the brain basis of cognitive
development. Previous studies have addressed the brain
mechanisms
development
(Arsalidou & Taylor, 2011; Zhou et al., 2007). However,
most of the previous studies have focused on isolated
brain regions. It remains unclear how developmental dif-
ference in large-scale brain modules facilitates the devel-
opment of arithmetical ability. Using graph theory, some
previous studies investigated the development of struc-
tural and resting-state functional brain networks from
childhood to adulthood and demonstrated that the task-
independent brain modules become more distinct, with
stronger connections within modules and weaker con-
nections between modules (Baum et al., 2017; Fair
et al., 2007; Gu et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2015). Such
modular segregation may allow for functional specializa-
tion and reduce competitive interference between brain
systems. However, almost all these previous studies just
focused on the development of task-independent brain
networks, and the findings were limited to cross-sectional
designs. Using task-based fMRI and a longitudinal
design, the present study extended the previous findings
by showing longitudinal increases in large-scale modular
segregation for a multiplication task during childhood
and adolescence, providing new insights into potential
neural mechanisms underlying the improvement of arith-
metic skill across development.

The present study found that the task-state brain mod-
ules became increasingly segregated with age. Specifi-
cally, the intra-connectivity within both the DMN and
FPN increased significantly from age 10 to 12, whereas
the inter-connectivity between the DMN and VN
decreased significantly at the same age period. Moreover,
the improvement in arithmetic ability from age 10 to
12 was associated with change in network segregation of
the DMN, and individual difference in arithmetic ability

| Developmental change in DMN

Many previous resting-state imaging studies have shown
that the intra-module connectivity of the DMN increased
significantly during the school-age period of development
(de Bie et al., 2012; Fair et al., 2008; Mak et al., 2017;
Supekar et al., 2010). Similarly, diffusion imaging studies
have revealed that the structural connectivity within the
DMN increased significantly with age during the school
years (Clayden et al., 2012; Supekar et al., 2010; Tamnes

et al., 2010). Moreover, functional connectivity of the
DMN was found positively associated with white matter
in a sample of 9–13 year old (Gordon
integrity
et al., 2011), suggesting that the structural connectivity of
the DMN may underlie functional connectivity develop-
ment of this system during childhood and adolescence.
The present study provides novel evidence for the
increased intra-module DMN connectivity for task-based
brain network development, suggesting a consistent
developmental trend in resting-state, structural and task-
based functional connectivity in the DMN.

We also observed decrease in inter-module connectiv-
ity between the DMN and the VN. A previous task-state
fMRI study for selective encoding of visual information
has shown that the functional coupling between the
DMN and the visual cortical areas is important for task-
irrelevant
&
Gazzaley, 2011). Hence, it is possible that reduced func-
tional coupling between the DMN and the VN contrib-
utes to more efficiency in processing task-irrelevant
information, thereby facilitating arithmetic processing by
putting more efforts into task-relevant information. Nota-
bly, the changes in both the intra- and inter-module con-
nectivity of the DMN were present from age 10 to 12 but
not from age 12 to 14, suggesting that the development of
DMN connectivity may be partly age-dependent.

| Developmental change in FPN

The present results about FPN connectivity are also con-
sistent with the previous cross-sectional studies examin-
ing functional connectivity development (Emerson &
Cantlon,
2007; Rosenberg-Lee
et al., 2011). For instance, Fair et al. (2007) reported
stronger resting-state functional connectivity between the
dorsolateral prefrontal and posterior parietal areas in
adolescence aged 10–15 years compared with children
aged 7–9 years. With the use of
task-based fMRI,
Rosenberg-Lee et al. (2011) reported greater functional
connectivity between the frontal and parietal regions in
children aged 8–9 years than those aged 7–8 years per-
forming an addition task. Chang et al.
(2016) also
observed increased prefrontal-parietal functional connec-
tivity during an addition task performance in adolescents
compared with children. Consistently, the present longi-
tudinal study showed a developmental increase in the
intra-module connectivity within the FPN, reflecting a
strengthening communication and information transmis-
sion within the frontal and parietal nodes for arithmetic
processing. Furthermore,
the increased intra-module
connectivity may suggest an enhanced importance of the

whole frontal-parietal module rather than local frontal
and parietal nodes. It should be noticed that the develop-
mental increase in the FPN connectivity was significant
from age 10 to 12 but with only a trend from age 12 to
14, indicating that such developmental progress may be
partly age-dependent.

Accumulating evidence suggests that functional connec-
tivity of the DMN correlates with individual difference in
multiple cognitive functions including working memory
(Sala-Llonch et al., 2012), creativity (Beaty et al., 2014),
mental manipulation (Yang et al., 2013) and language
processing in adults (Yang et al., 2013). All these cogni-
tive functions are closely related to arithmetic processing.
Importantly, the present study found that the enhanced
modular segregation of the DMN over time was positively
correlated with individual difference in the arithmetic
improvement, suggesting that the development of DMN
topology may serve as a neural substrate for supporting
greater improvement in arithmetic ability. It is possible
that the DMN re-configures with age, becoming more
functional specialized and more efficient in coordination
with other brain modules for arithmetic processing. Addi-
tionally, this brain–behaviour relationship holds even
when general intelligence and performance of the control
condition were controlled, indicating that the correlation
might not be simply attributed to difference in general
cognitive abilities. Hence,
the development of DMN
topology may exhibit partial specificity for arithmetic
processing.

The role of the FPN in individual difference in arith-
metic ability in children remains largely unknown in the
extant literature. Previous developmental studies have
shown some evidence that greater activation of the fron-
tal and parietal regions is associated with better perfor-
mance in various high-order cognitive tasks in samples
with a wider age range or in older individuals (Klingberg
et al., 2002; Olesen et al., 2007; Rubia et al., 2006). When
restricted to a narrow age
range, Spencer-Smith
et al. (2013) found that activation of the frontal and parie-
tal regions was positively correlated with performance
during a delayed match-to-sample task in children aged
10–12 years but not in those aged 7–9 years. Similarly,
Price et al. (2013) reported a positive correlation between
activation in the left parietal region and performance
during an arithmetic task in adolescents, whereas no
such an association was detected in younger children.
Altogether, the role of the FPN in high-order cognitive
functions including arithmetic ability may vary with age.

The lack of a significant correlation between frontal-
parietal activation and high-order cognitive performance
at younger ages may be attributable to the protracted
development of the FPN (Crone et al., 2006; Giedd &
Rapoport, 2010). In consistence, the present study found
a significant correlation between the intra-module con-
nections of the FPN and performance on the outside-
scanner multiplication task at T2 but not at T1. The sig-
nificant correlation suggests that brain network topology
of the FPN can serve as a substrate for supporting good
arithmetic performance. When further dividing the chil-
dren into younger and older age groups, the correlation
at T2 was significant for the older group but not for the
younger group, providing further evidence that the role
of the FPN in arithmetic processing may be age depen-
dent. Further longitudinal studies with larger sample size
and multiple time points would be needed to distinguish
the FPN in arithmetic ability across
the role of
different ages.

A number of caveats need to be noted. First, several
recent studies have raised that head motion artefacts can
to connectivity estimates
introduce systematic bias
(Parkes et al., 2018; Power et al., 2014). The present study
found no significant differences in head motion between
age groups and no significant correlations between head
motion and performance on the multiplication task. Fur-
thermore, including head motion in the statistical ana-
lyses as a covariate did not alter the results reported in
the present study. Therefore, the observed effects were
not likely due to artefacts produced by head motion. Sec-
ond, although we use methods described above to extract
time points corresponding to the multiplication trials, the
time series from the multiplication trials and control tri-
als could not be completely separated due to the continu-
ity of signals. However, this limitation may have limited
effects on our results, because we were mainly focused
on developmental difference, and the signal-extraction
method was the same for both the younger and older
groups and for both Time 1 and Time 2. Moreover, the
present study found a significant correlation between
change in brain network connectivity and arithmetic gain
when general intelligence and performance of the control
condition was included as covariates, providing further
evidence that large-scale brain network connectivity may
support arithmetic development. Lastly, our study aimed
to investigate developmental change in large-scale brain
modules and its relationship with arithmetic ability.
Though our findings were highly consistent with findings
task-independent neuroimaging studies
in previous

(Baum et al., 2017; Sherman et al., 2014) and supported
our hypothesis, it remains unclear whether the neuro-
development of the FPN and DMN may play a similar
role in the development of other high-order cognitive
abilities. Future study should conduct a battery of cogni-
tive tasks inside the MRI scanner to address the role of
large-scale brain modules in cognitive development more
comprehensively.

human brain is topologically organized into an efficient
network architecture that can be divided into a set of spa-
tially distributed but
functionally relevant modules
(Power et al., 2011; Rubinov & Sporns, 2010; Zuo
et al., 2017). Integration and interactions among these
brain modules have been suggested to contribute to
behavioural performance in a variety of high-order cogni-
tive functions (Cole et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Power
et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2020). Therefore, studying brain
connectivity across different brain modules in children
may enhance our understanding of arithmetic develop-
ment. Although several recent studies have used brain
connectivity analysis to examine arithmetic processing in
children, most of the studies have focused on brain con-
nectivity of particular seed regions (Chang et al., 2016;
Emerson & Cantlon, 2012; Supekar et al., 2013). Knowl-
edge is still limited regarding developmental change in

different brain modules. Graph theory, which describes
different regions of the brain as nodes and region-to-
region correlations as edges, has been utilized as a popu-
lar approach with a powerful statistical framework for
investigating integration and interactions among multi-

Another limitation in previous imaging studies about
arithmetic development is that they often employed a
cross-sectional design. It should be noticed that the cross-
sectional studies included participants from different
ages, families and social backgrounds. Large individual
variability should be a major concern. Hence, it was pos-
sible that these studies failed to detect or falsely suggested
changes over time (Casey et al., 2005). Accordingly, to
reduce the influence of
individual variability and to
increase statistical power, the longitudinal approach is
recommended. As for the development in brain network
topology,
studies have
employed longitudinal fMRI datasets comprising children
at different ages (Fan et al., 2021; Sherman et al., 2014),
to the best of our knowledge, no study has addressed lon-
gitudinal changes in multiple brain network modules for
arithmetic development.

The present study aimed to employ graph theory to
examine the longitudinal development of
large-scale
brain network modules for arithmetic ability and delin-
eate its role in arithmetic development. To do so, we
analysed a public longitudinal dataset entitled ‘Brain

formed several cognitive tasks inside or outside the MRI
scanner at age of 8–14 years old (Time 1) and once again

at an average of 2.2 years later (Time 2). In this study, we
mainly focused on the task-state fMRI data involving a
multiplication task inside the scanner at both time
points. In light of previous findings in task-independent
brain network development (Baum et al., 2017; Fair
et al., 2007), we hypothesized that some of the task-state
functional brain modules would become increasingly seg-
regated with age, driven by both increased within-
module connections and decreased between-module con-
nections. Given the critical role of the FPN and DMN in
arithmetic processing
(Emerson & Cantlon, 2012;

comprehensive understanding of the cognitive implica-

comparison and other math skills. Further investigation
of this public dataset is still of great value.
